newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Motorbike maker KTM H1 pretax up 12 pct.
newsitem.headline: Motorbike maker KTM H1 pretax up 12 pct.

text.p: Austria's sole motorbike maker KTM on Monday posted a gleaming 12 percent rise in pretax profit to 57 million schillings ($4.7 million) for the first half of 1996/97 and forecast even better results for the second half.
"We expect to reach the same turnover in the second half and even better pre-tax profit than in the first half of the year," chief executive Stefan Pierer told a news conference.
Group sales of KTM Motorradholding AG climbed 23 percent to 615 million schillings in the first six months to August 31 1996, compared to 502 million in the year ago period.
Last year 1995/96 turnover exceeded one billion schillings for the first time in the company's history and pre-tax profit reached 102 million.
KTM, the youngest stock on the Vienna Stock Exchange, has far outperformed the ATX blue chip index since it was listed on December 12 last year at 590 schillings.
At 1035 GMT on Friday KTM shares were trading at 709 schillings, a 20 percent gain on their starting price, while the ATX rose just 7.5 percent in the same time to 1,208.06.

Since it was rescued from insolvency in 1991, KTM has carved out a lucrative niche for itself in the European and U.S. leisure sport markets with "hard endurance" bikes that perform as well "off-piste" as they do on tarmac.
Motorbike sales in the first half rose to 9,280, against 8,017 the previous year. Racing bikes accounted for 60 percent of sales, with hard endurance bikes notching up 33 percent.
KTM said the second half had already got off to a good start due to high order intake and supply capacity. In March alone over 2,000 bikes were sold, bringing in a turnover of 134 million schillings.
"The first weeks of the second half have been extremely encouraging. We have already reached last year's quota," said Pierer.
KTM said its export share currently stood at 92 percent, with the United States and Germany, where hard endurance bikes are particularly popular, the biggest markets.
KTM's "mini bikes" for children, on the market since January, had also seen a large order intake.
The company recently established new importers in Malaysia and the Philippines and said the first orders would be delivered in the second half.
"We see great potential for growth in the far Eastern markets," it said.
In addition, KTM said it had just acquired a 75 percent stake in a Dutch manufacturer of suspension parts.
"It is a strategic deal for us as we are a small producer compared to other big companies in Europe," said Pierer. ($ = 12.18 Austrian Schillings)
